title: S29 The You Do's core method is likely to crash the first time Lucía tests it, and nothing on the page explains why.
description:
[I] The You Do's core method is likely to crash the first time Lucía tests it, and nothing on the page explains why. `insert_decision_with_evidence` must do «BEGIN → decisión → lastrowid → evidence → COMMIT», as every demo does with `con.execute("BEGIN")`. Every demo issues `BEGIN` right after DDL, where Python's `sqlite3` has no transaction open. In the You Do she must first seed `entities` and `candidate_pairs` with ordinary `INSERT`s, which (by default) silently open an implicit transaction. Her explicit `BEGIN` then raises `OperationalError: cannot start a transaction within a transaction`. A grep of S12 and S29 finds 0 hits for `isolation_level`, `autocommit` or «implícit».

Dónde (campo del contenido): `youDo.starterCode` (`insert_decision_with_evidence` comment), `youDo.requirements[6]`, `theory[6].code`

repro:
1. Abrir S29 (mlops)
2. Pestaña youdo
3. Ubicar `youDo.starterCode` (`insert_decision_with_evidence` comment), `youDo.requirements[6]`, `theory[6].code`
improvement: `src/lib/course/sections/s29-mlops.ts`: teach one pattern explicitly. Either `with con:` (a context manager that commits or rolls back), or `con.commit()` after seeding plus a callout: «el módulo sqlite3 abre una transacción implícita antes de un INSERT; haz commit del seed antes de tu BEGIN». Add a We Do whose starter has this exact bug. (The error message is cryptic, and it lands on the method that carries the section's main invariant.)

title: S33 The tie-breaking rule is taught as a general property of `max`, but it is an accident of set ordering.
description:
[I] The tie-breaking rule is taught as a general property of `max`, but it is an accident of set ordering. The You Do labels `y=[1,1,0,0]` are exactly a tie, so this matters. `max(set(y), key=y.count)` returns the first maximal element in set-iteration order. For `{0, 1}` that happens to be 0, but it is not "the smaller class" in general: `y=[1,8,1,8]` returns 8 under CPython 3.12, and for strings the result depends on hash randomisation.

Dónde (campo del contenido): `theory[3].code.code` comment, `theory[3].paragraphs[2]`

Dónde (campo del contenido): `youDo.starterCode` (`before_path`, `after_path`, `ok_same`), `youDo.objectives[1]`

Compute `same_result = before == after` and `recall = len(after & before) / len(before)`, and include a key choice that loses matches so the gate can go red. (A gate that cannot fail is a tautological test; AGENTS.md calls these worse than no test.)

CP-N3-C (`BRIEF.md`, `RUBRIC.json.tests_required`, `catalog.ts`) requires «baseline determinista», «calibración reportada», «umbral por costo → revisión humana», «no fuga de datos» (train/eval separation), «desempeño por subgrupo», «abstención soportada» and the interface `triage.score(case) -> TriageDecision`. Its P0s include «Sin calibración» and «Fuga de datos». The S39 You Do starter's "model" is `score = min(1.0, 0.35 + 0.45 * bool(case["shared_signal"]))`. It has no training data, no baseline, no calibration, no cost-based threshold, no split and no per-subgroup performance, and it exposes `triage(case, *, threshold, …) -> Tuple`. S39's own tagline promises «con baseline, calibración, abstención». Calibration and baselines were taught in S33–S35 (grep `calibra` S34: 99 hits, `baseline` S33: 97), but S39 never asks her to reuse them.
